section.title: A Good Soldier of Christ Jesus
section.sectionRationale: Having charged Timothy to guard the deposit, Paul now shows him how to carry and pass it on: be strong in grace, entrust the message to reliable teachers, and endure hardship. Three everyday pictures, the soldier, the athlete, and the farmer, teach single-minded, disciplined, patient endurance. All of it is anchored in the risen Christ and sealed by a trustworthy saying about dying, living, enduring, and God's unbreakable faithfulness.
section.thesis: Strengthened by grace, Timothy is to endure hardship like a focused soldier, a rule-keeping athlete, and a hardworking farmer, remembering the risen Christ for whose gospel Paul suffers in chains, and resting in the trustworthy saying that those who die and endure with Christ will live and reign with Him, for even when we are faithless He remains faithful.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the call to be strong in grace and entrust the gospel to faithful men; the three images of the soldier, athlete, and farmer that model endurance; and the risen Christ at the center, sealed by the trustworthy saying of verses 11 to 13.

units.label: Be strong and entrust the gospel

verses.text: You therefore, my child, {{endynamoo|be strong}} in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.
And the things that you have heard me say among many witnesses, {{paratithemi|entrust}} these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well.
Join me in suffering, like a good {{stratiotes|soldier}} of Christ Jesus.
A soldier refrains from entangling himself in civilian affairs, in order to please the one who enlisted him.
Likewise, a competitor does not receive the crown unless he competes according to the rules.
The hardworking farmer should be the first to partake of the crops.
Consider what I am saying, for the Lord will give you insight into all things.
Remember Jesus Christ, {{egeiro|raised from the dead}}, descended from David, as proclaimed by my gospel,
for which I suffer to the extent of being chained like a criminal. But the word of God cannot be chained!
For this reason I endure all things for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory.
This is a trustworthy saying: If we died with Him, we will also live with Him;
if we endure, we will also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He will also deny us;
if we are faithless, He remains {{pistos|faithful}}, for He cannot deny Himself.

endynamoo.gloss: To be strengthened, to be empowered from within. The form is passive: Timothy is to let himself be made strong, and the strength is located in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, not in his own resolve. Endurance in ministry begins not with gritted teeth but with drawing on the grace God supplies.

paratithemi.gloss: To place beside, to deposit or entrust for safekeeping. It is the verb behind the noun deposit in chapter 1: Timothy commits the apostolic message to trustworthy people as one hands over a treasure. Here it maps a chain of four generations, Paul to Timothy to faithful men to others, the ordinary way the gospel is preserved.

stratiotes.gloss: A soldier. Paul draws on the soldier's single-minded devotion: an enlisted man does not tangle himself in civilian pursuits but aims to please his commanding officer. The Christian worker, likewise, accepts hardship and keeps focus, serving the One who enlisted him rather than being pulled apart by lesser concerns.

egeiro.gloss: To raise up, to wake from the dead. The perfect tense in remember Jesus Christ raised from the dead points to a past event with abiding effect: He was raised and remains the living Lord. This risen Christ, the promised offspring of David, is the sum of Paul's gospel and the ground of all endurance.

pistos.gloss: Faithful, trustworthy, reliable. The word describes the trustworthy saying, the faithful men who receive the deposit, and supremely Christ Himself, who remains faithful even when we are faithless. God's faithfulness is not propped up by ours; it rests on His own unchanging character, for He cannot deny Himself.

basic.context: Paul keeps coaching Timothy for hard ministry. First he tells him to draw strength from God's grace and to pass the gospel on to reliable people who can teach others. Then he uses three familiar pictures, a soldier, an athlete, and a farmer, to show that faithful service means focus, discipline, and hard work. At the center he points to the risen Jesus, and he ends with a memorable saying about staying with Christ through death and hardship.
basic.hermeneutics: The three images are illustrations, not rigid rules, and together they teach one lesson: gospel work costs something and calls for endurance. The trustworthy saying in verses 11 to 13 is likely an early Christian hymn or creed, quoted here to steady believers who are tempted to give up under pressure.
basic.originalLanguages: Timothy is to endynamoo, to be strengthened, in grace, a passive verb that points to strength received, not summoned. He is to paratithemi, to entrust, the message like a deposit. The soldier is a stratiotes, single-minded for his commander. Paul says to remember Christ egeiro, raised from the dead, the risen Lord. And even when we are faithless, God remains pistos, faithful, true to Himself.
basic.typology: Jesus as the offspring of David who is raised from the dead fulfills God's promise of an everlasting king. The soldier, athlete, and farmer picture the believer's whole life of disciplined service that leads to reward.
basic.christ: Everything centers on Jesus Christ, risen from the dead and descended from David, the heart of Paul's gospel. Union with Him is the theme of the closing saying: die with Him and live with Him, endure and reign with Him. He is so faithful that He cannot deny His own nature or His own people.
basic.god: God supplies grace that makes His servants strong, spreads His word so freely that no chain can bind it, and remains faithful even when His people falter. His purpose is the salvation and eternal glory of His elect.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 1 also names Jesus as descended from David and declared Son of God by resurrection. First Corinthians 9 pictures the disciplined athlete running to win. Romans 8 promises that if we suffer with Christ we will be glorified with Him.
basic.oneStory: God promised David a son whose kingdom would never end, and that promise lands in the risen Jesus. Now His unstoppable word runs out to gather the elect, carried by servants who endure like soldiers, athletes, and farmers, until they live and reign with the faithful Christ forever.

context.literary:
Chapter 2 opens with a contrast carried by one small word. Chapter 1 ended with those who deserted Paul; chapter 2 begins 'You therefore,' and the 'therefore' draws a line from that failure to Timothy's task. The passage then has a clear shape. Verses 1 and 2 give the foundation and the method, strength from grace and a chain of teaching. Verses 3 to 7 are three pictures, soldier, competitor and farmer, each introduced in a single sentence and each followed by Paul's own call to think about them. Verses 8 to 10 name the content and cost of the gospel. Verses 11 to 13 close with a short poem.

The three pictures are linked by what each of them wants at the end. The soldier wants to please the one who enlisted him, the competitor wants the crown, and the farmer wants his share of the harvest. All three have a goal that is only reached by work: single focus, obedience to rules, and labour. After the third Paul says 'Consider what I am saying,' and the commentary is held back, as though he trusts Timothy to draw the lesson once the pictures are in his mind.

The saying of verses 11 to 13 is introduced with a formula Paul uses five times in the Pastoral Letters, 'This is a trustworthy saying,' and its balance is deliberate. It has four 'if' clauses. The first two are positive, dying and enduring, with a matching promise of life and reigning. The third is a warning, denial and being denied. The fourth, about faithlessness, turns back to comfort, but with a reason attached. The saying ends on the nature of God, and the chapter's argument has moved from what Timothy must do to what God is.

Verse 8 sits at the centre of the passage. Between the exhortation of verses 1 to 7 and the saying of verses 11 to 13, Paul places a command to remember Jesus Christ, raised and descended from David. Everything else is arranged around that remembering.
context.historical:
The images Paul uses were drawn from the everyday experience of the Roman world. Roman soldiers were conspicuous in every provincial city, and the guards who held Paul in Rome were themselves soldiers, Acts 28:16. A soldier on service gave up his ordinary trade and was supported by the state; hence the point of 'civilian affairs,' the ordinary business of making a living. A soldier who was distracted by farming or trading was not wholly his commander's man.

Athletic games were central to Greek and Roman life, and Paul uses them often, as in 1 Corinthians 9:24-27. Competitors who broke the rules of the contest could be disqualified however fast they ran, which is the force of competing 'according to the rules.' The prize itself was a wreath, which is why Paul calls it a 'crown,' and in 1 Corinthians 9:25 he contrasts a perishable wreath with an imperishable one.

The farmer was the most familiar figure of all, since most people in the empire lived off the land. The laborer who worked the field had the first right to the harvest, and Paul uses the same principle in 1 Corinthians 9:10, where the plowman expects to share in the crop.

Paul's own situation sets the tone. He is 'chained like a criminal,' verse 9, in a Rome where an apostle who had once been received as a visitor now has to be searched for, 2 Timothy 1:17. Yet the word is not chained. Acts 28:30-31 closes on the same truth, with Paul preaching boldly and without hindrance even while under guard. The church Timothy leads is small, scattered and under pressure, so a passage about endurance, delegation and the faithfulness of a risen King would have been heard as urgent practical help.
context.canonical:
The charge to 'be strong' is an old one. It is the word God gives Joshua at the start of his leadership in Joshua 1:6-9, where the command to be strong and courageous is followed by the promise that the LORD will be with him wherever he goes. Paul takes the same posture and moves its source: Timothy is to be strong 'in the grace that is in Christ Jesus,' and Ephesians 6:10 says the same, 'be strong in the Lord and in His mighty power.'

The three images recur elsewhere in Paul. Epaphroditus is a 'fellow soldier,' Philippians 2:25, and Paul tells the Ephesians to put on the armor of God, Ephesians 6:10-17. The runner appears in 1 Corinthians 9:24-27 and again in 2 Timothy 4:7, where Paul says 'I have finished the race.' The farmer appears in 1 Corinthians 9:10 and in the parables of Jesus.

Verse 8 reaches back to the promise to David. In 2 Samuel 7:12-13 God says He will raise up David's descendant and establish his throne forever, and Psalm 132:11 speaks of the same oath. Peter uses this in his sermon at Pentecost, saying that David foresaw the resurrection of the Christ, Acts 2:30-31, and Romans 1:3-4 pairs the Davidic descent with the resurrection in the same way Paul does here. Isaiah 11:1 and Revelation 5:5 carry the same line to its conclusion.

The closing saying has strong links to Jesus' own words. 'If we deny Him, He will also deny us' recalls Matthew 10:33, and the promise of reigning recalls Revelation 3:21, where the overcomer shares Christ's throne. 'We died with Him' belongs to Romans 6:8 and Colossians 2:12, where the believer's baptism is a sharing in Christ's death and raising. The last line, that God cannot deny Himself, has the same ground as Numbers 23:19 and Romans 3:3-4, where human unfaithfulness does not cancel what God has said.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul intends Timothy to think of ministry as a relay, not a performance. The gospel was heard 'among many witnesses,' and it is to be handed on to others who will in turn teach. The measure of success is not Timothy's own influence but the presence of faithful and qualified people four steps down the line, from Paul to Timothy, to faithful men, to others. A teacher who has no successors has only done half the job.

The three pictures are also meant to be taken together. A soldier alone would suggest harshness, an athlete alone would suggest competition, and a farmer alone might suggest only patience. Together they say that gospel service needs focus, honesty and hard labour, and that reward comes to the one who stays with these.

Paul's greatest concern is that Timothy will not collapse under cost. This is why the hymn is so placed. A person who is told to endure needs to know what endurance leads to and what stands behind it. The risen Christ, the kingly descendant of David, is the pledge that suffering is not the end of the story, and the promise that He cannot deny Himself is meant to hold Timothy up on the days when his own faith feels thin.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The commands in this passage are plain: be strong in grace, entrust the teaching to faithful men, share in suffering, think carefully about what has been said, and remember Jesus Christ. They apply to all who hand on the gospel, not only pastors. Parents, teachers, mentors and friends all stand somewhere in the chain of verse 2.

The three images need care. They are comparisons, not a complete theory of Christian life. Reading the soldier as a call to withdraw from all ordinary work would conflict with Paul's own tentmaking, Acts 18:3, and with his instruction elsewhere to work with one's hands, 1 Thessalonians 4:11. Reading the athlete as a promise that those who train hardest will always win would turn a picture of discipline into a promise of prosperity. The point of each is narrow: the soldier shows devotion to a single purpose, the competitor shows obedience to the rules of the game, and the farmer shows that labour comes before reward.

The closing saying is a quotation which describes what is true of Christ and His people; it is not a list of commands. It should be read as a statement of how things stand between Christ and those who belong to Him, and then used as a basis for encouragement and warning.

debates.question: What does 'if we deny Him, He will also deny us' mean for a believer?

views.label: A real warning that a believer could lose salvation
views.case: On this view the line is a straightforward statement that a person who finally rejects Christ is rejected by Him, in line with Matthew 10:33 and Hebrews 3:14, where holding firm to the end is the sign of sharing in Christ. The four 'if' clauses are then all to be read as real conditions. Those who take this reading stress that Paul has just urged endurance, and that the warning gives the exhortation its seriousness.

views.label: A description of those who were never truly His
views.case: Others read the line as describing final, settled denial, which shows a person never really belonged. They point to 1 John 2:19, 'if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us,' and to promises like John 10:28 that no one will snatch Christ's sheep from His hand. In this reading perseverance is the evidence of true faith, and apostasy is the evidence of its absence.

views.label: A warning against the shame of denial that is not final
views.case: A third reading separates the settled denial of the unbeliever from the stumbling of a Christian. Peter denied Jesus three times, Luke 22:61-62, and was restored, John 21:15-17. On this view the line warns of real loss, including loss of reward and of public confession's fruit, while the next verse protects the believer who is faithless but still belongs to Christ.

debates.bearing: The verb in verse 12 is the same one Jesus uses in Matthew 10:33, so the saying has His authority behind it. All three readings agree that the warning is serious and that endurance is not optional. They differ on whether it is addressed to those who may lose what they have or to those who show they never had it.

debates.question: Is verses 11 to 13 an early hymn or creed?

views.label: A quoted hymn
views.case: The saying's tight parallelism, the repeated 'if' and 'we will,' and the formula 'This is a trustworthy saying' suggest a piece of early Christian worship that Paul quotes. Its content, dying and rising with Christ, fits what was said at baptism, Romans 6:3-4.

views.label: Paul's own composition
views.case: Others argue that the form is Paul's own, a rhetorical triplet in his usual style. The vocabulary is closely linked to his language elsewhere, such as 'died with' and 'live with' in Romans 6:8, and it uses ideas from his other letters. The 'trustworthy saying' formula can introduce something he has just made.

views.label: Impossible to tell
views.case: Some readers say the evidence does not allow certainty and that the question matters less than the meaning. A saying is trustworthy whether it was composed in a church service or at Paul's desk.

debates.bearing: Whether it is a quotation or not, Paul vouches for it and uses it as the settled shape of the Christian life, so its authority is the same.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's first command is endynamoo, 'be strong,' in a form that is passive in sense: 'be made strong,' or 'be empowered.' The same verb appears in Ephesians 6:10, Philippians 4:13 and 1 Timothy 1:12, always with the source of strength outside the believer. The sphere is 'the grace that is in Christ Jesus,' so grace is not only forgiveness at the start but the sphere of strength for the whole of life.

In verse 2 'entrust' is paratithemi, 'to place alongside,' the verb of the banker's deposit and the same idea that stood behind the 'deposit' of 1 Timothy 6:20 and 2 Timothy 1:14. It is the same verb Jesus used on the cross when He entrusted His spirit to the Father, Luke 23:46. The phrase 'many witnesses' can mean 'in the presence of' many or 'through the agency of' many, a small ambiguity in the Greek; either way it points to public, checked teaching, not secret tradition.

'Join me in suffering,' verse 3, is a single compound verb, synkakopatheo, 'suffer hardship together.' It is the same verb Paul used in 1:8, and it occurs in the New Testament only in these two verses. Paul is not asking Timothy to hunt for pain; he is asking him not to step back from a shared lot. 'Hardworking' of the farmer is kopiao, to labour to the point of weariness, a word Paul also uses for his own work in Colossians 1:29.

In verse 8 the participle 'raised' is a perfect passive, egegermenon, which describes a state that began and continues. Jesus is the One who was raised and is still the Risen One. 'Descended from David' is literally 'from the seed of David,' the same wording as Romans 1:3. The word translated 'criminal' in verse 9 is kakourgos, the term Luke uses of the two men crucified beside Jesus, Luke 23:32. Paul's chains put him in the same category in the eyes of the world as Jesus on the cross.

'Endure' in verses 10 and 12 is hypomeno, to remain under, to stay put under a load. It is the word of Matthew 10:22, 'the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.' The last pair of clauses uses the verbs of faith and unfaith. 'Faithless' is apisteo, the verb used in Romans 3:3 of those 'who did not have faith.' The contrast with 'faithful,' pistos, is the heart of the final line. Humans can be apistos; God, because He cannot deny Himself, cannot be. The verb 'deny' is arneomai, the same as in Matthew 10:33.

typology.fulfillment: God's promise to David that a descendant would be raised up to rule forever had a first, partial fulfilment in Solomon, who built the house for God's Name. The writers of the New Testament see it reach its true shape in Jesus. Peter says David, being a prophet, 'spoke about the resurrection of the Christ,' Acts 2:30-31, and Paul pairs descent from David with resurrection from the dead in Romans 1:3-4 and here. The escalation is that the throne is no longer held by a man who dies and rests with his fathers but by one who has been raised and lives. The type falls short in Solomon, whose own heart turned away, 1 Kings 11.

typology.type: Joshua, strong and courageous before the conquest
typology.fulfillment: Joshua was told to be strong and courageous because the LORD was with him as he led Israel into the land, Joshua 1:6-9. Timothy's task is a different kind of conquest, a mission in which the 'land' is people brought to Christ and the fight is spiritual, Ephesians 6:10-17. The pattern of a leader who is commissioned, told to be strong and promised the presence of God carries over. The escalation is that Christ is the greater Joshua, giving a rest that the first could not, Hebrews 4:8-9, and that the strength Timothy needs is the grace that is in Him, not a resolve he must summon. The type falls short in that Joshua's battles were with swords and Timothy's are not.

typology.type: David hunted before he reigned, 1 Samuel 22:1-2
typology.fulfillment: David was anointed as king long before he sat on a throne and spent years in hiding while distressed people gathered around him. The pattern, suffering first and reigning after, shapes the saying of verse 12, 'if we endure, we will also reign with Him.' Jesus fulfils it in His death and rising, and the book of Revelation promises believers a share in the reign: 'to the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to sit with Me on My throne,' Revelation 3:21. The correspondence is helpful for how believers should read their own hardships. It breaks down at an important point: David's suffering was not redemptive, while Christ's was, and the believer's reign is derived from His.

study.christ:
This passage meets Christ in an unusual place: not in a prophecy being fulfilled or in a miracle, but in a command to remember Him. 'Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David, as proclaimed by my gospel.' Paul gives Timothy two facts about Jesus and calls them his gospel. The first, that He was descended from David, says that Jesus is the promised King. The second, that He is risen, says that this King has overcome the one enemy no king could. The gospel is not a set of ideals but a Person with a lineage and a resurrection, and the whole letter's call to endure stands on those two facts.

The Davidic line matters because of what God swore. In 2 Samuel 7:12-13 and Psalm 132:11 He promised to place one of David's descendants on the throne forever, and Jesus Himself pressed the question of whose son the Christ is, Matthew 22:42. To say 'descended from David' is to say that all the hope of Israel for a righteous king has a particular person who answers it. Isaiah 11:1 spoke of a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and Revelation 5:5 calls Jesus the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, who has triumphed.

The resurrection matters because without it the Davidic claim would be a dead hope. Peter's sermon at Pentecost joins the two: the oath to David pointed to the Christ, and the resurrection shows that the oath was kept, Acts 2:30-31. A king who stays in the grave cannot reign forever, but this King has been raised, and because He lives the promise is secure.

The closing saying then places believers inside that story. 'If we died with Him, we will also live with Him' is the way Paul describes union with Christ in Romans 6:8, where being baptised into His death means walking in newness of life. 'If we endure, we will also reign with Him' fits Revelation 3:21. 'If we deny Him, He will also deny us' repeats the warning of Jesus in Matthew 10:33. And 'He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself' describes who Christ is. He does not change His mind about those who are in Him, because to do so would be to contradict His own nature.

Paul's own situation adds a pattern. He is chained like a criminal, verse 9, yet he describes the word as free, and the same man who is suffering says that all this is 'for the sake of the elect,' verse 10. In this he reflects the pattern of Christ who suffered for His people, though with an important limit. Paul's suffering helps bring the message to others. It does not obtain their salvation, since the salvation is already 'in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory.' A reader should take care not to read verse 10 as if the apostle completed what Christ lacked, and should let the phrase 'in Christ Jesus' control the sentence.
study.god:
This passage shows a God whose grace is a source of strength. The command to Timothy to be strong in grace assumes that God's favour is not only a pardon but a supply, and that He gives it to people who feel weak. It is 'the grace that is in Christ Jesus,' not something kept in reserve for an elite. For worship, this means that weakness is a place to meet God and not a thing to hide from Him.

He is also a God whose word cannot be stopped. 'The word of God cannot be chained,' verse 9, and the surrounding passages of Scripture say the same: it 'will accomplish what I please,' Isaiah 55:11, and 'the word of our God stands forever,' Isaiah 40:8. Roman chains held the apostle but not what the apostle preached. The book of Acts ends on the same note, with the word spreading while Paul is under guard, Acts 28:30-31. God chooses to work through weak messengers, but the power is in the message and in the One who stands behind it.

He is a God who has chosen. The 'elect' of verse 10 are not an afterthought; Paul endures because he knows God has a people to bring in, and his patience is fuelled by that. The doctrine of election here is not abstract. It does not discourage evangelism but gives it grounds, since the work will not be in vain. Titus 1:1 shows the same link between God's elect and the knowledge of the truth.

He is faithful, and the final line makes the weight of this clear. 'If we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.' Numbers 23:19 says that God is not a man that He should lie or change His mind, and Romans 3:3-4 asks whether human unbelief can cancel God's faithfulness, and answers, 'Certainly not!' This faithfulness is not indifference to sin, because the previous clause says that those who deny Him will be denied. It is the steadfastness of a God who is true to what He has said, including both His promises and His warnings. The same constancy that comforts the weak believer humbles the one who presumes.

The passage also says something about God and suffering. God does not remove Timothy from hardship; He joins him to it. The call to 'join me in suffering' comes alongside the promise that the Lord will give insight, verse 7. This is a God who gives understanding for a hard path rather than a way around it. It also fits Philippians 1:29, where suffering for Christ is something granted, and Acts 14:22, which says that we must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom.

Finally, the passage shows a God who is revealed in a Person. Paul's gospel is summed up in Jesus Christ, raised and descended from David. God is not known in this passage through an argument but in the face of One who has died and lives. The right response is the one the saying itself models, to remember Him and to sing.

crossReferences.note: God's charge to Joshua to be strong and courageous because the LORD is with him. It is the Old Testament model for 2 Timothy 2:1. In both, a younger leader takes up a task after a great predecessor, and the strength is a promise of God's presence, not a personality trait.

Paul's fullest picture of the soldier, with the believer to be strong in the Lord and in His mighty power and to put on the armor of God. It explains 2 Timothy 2:3-4: the soldier's single purpose is spiritual warfare, and the equipment is given by God.

The best parallel for the competitor in 2 Timothy 2:5. Paul speaks of strict discipline for an imperishable crown and fears being disqualified after preaching to others. It shows that the athlete is a picture of self-discipline in service, not of the pursuit of personal glory.

Applies the principle of the plowman and the thresher sharing in the harvest to those who serve the gospel. It supports the farmer of 2 Timothy 2:6, who works hard and has a right to the fruit, and shows that Paul sees reward as part of the order God has set.

The promise of a Davidic descendant whose throne God will establish forever. It is the source for the phrase 'descended from David' in verse 8, and shows that Paul's summary of the gospel is built on a promise God made centuries earlier.

Peter explains that David, foreseeing the resurrection, spoke of the Christ, whose body saw no decay. It joins the Davidic promise and the resurrection in the same way as 2 Timothy 2:8, and shows that the pairing was part of the first apostolic preaching.

Describes the Son as a descendant of David according to the flesh and declared Son of God with power by His resurrection. It is the nearest parallel to verse 8, which suggests that Paul's brief summary of the gospel was standard across his letters.

'If we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with Him.' The first line of the trustworthy saying in verse 11 almost repeats it, and Romans 6:3-4 gives its meaning: dying with Christ begins in baptism and leads to a new way of living.

Jesus says that whoever denies Him before men, He will deny before His Father in heaven. It stands directly behind 2 Timothy 2:12 and uses the same verb, which suggests that Paul's line quotes or recalls the teaching of Jesus himself.

Promises the overcomer a place with Christ on His throne, just as He overcame. It fills in 'we will also reign with Him,' and shows that the reign of believers is a share in the victory of the One who endured first.

Asks whether human unbelief nullifies God's faithfulness and answers 'Certainly not!' It is the logic behind the final line of the saying, that God remains faithful even when His people are faithless, because He is true whatever men may be.

States that God is not a man who lies or changes His mind, and asks whether He will promise and not fulfil. It gives the Old Testament ground for 'He cannot deny Himself,' the character of a God whose word and nature do not come apart.

study.oneStory:
The Bible is a story of promises made and kept, and this passage stands at one of the places where the line of promise becomes visible. God told David that a descendant would sit on his throne forever, 2 Samuel 7:12-13. Centuries of Israel's failed kings seemed to cancel the promise, but the prophets kept it alive, and the New Testament shows it answered in Jesus. When Paul tells Timothy to remember Jesus 'descended from David,' he is calling on one of the Old Testament's central hopes. The seed promised to the woman in Genesis 3:15, to Abraham in Genesis 22:18 and to David in 2 Samuel 7 is a single seed.

The passage also answers a question the story keeps raising: how will God's rule reach the nations when His appointed king is rejected and killed? The answer in verses 8 to 10 is that the King has been raised, and that His word cannot be bound, so that the elect will obtain salvation. The empire's chains and the church's weakness do not stop the spread. This is the pattern of Acts, where the word of God continued to spread and multiply, Acts 12:24, and it is the pattern of history until the end.

It sets up the shape of the Christian life that the rest of the New Testament fills in. Believers have died with Christ and live with Him, they endure and will reign with Him, and the day of judgment is real. These are not new ideas, since from the start the story has been about a people who must choose between trust and distrust. In Eden the question was whether to believe God's word. In Israel it was whether to remain loyal in the wilderness. In the church it is whether to confess Christ before men. The saying of verses 11 to 13 applies that old question to the age of the church.

It also fits the larger theme of faithfulness. Humanity fails again and again, in Adam, in Israel's golden calf, in Peter's denial. Yet each time the story does not end there, because God remains faithful, and His faithfulness finally takes human shape in the faithful Son. This is why Paul can write that even if we are faithless He remains faithful: the one who stands at the center of history is not subject to the failures of His people.

The story ends in new creation, where the promise of reigning is finally fulfilled. Revelation 22:5 says that God's servants will reign forever, and the throne of David's Son becomes the throne of God and of the Lamb. The soldier receives his discharge, the competitor his crown and the farmer his share of the harvest, and those who died with Christ live with Him in the world that has no more death.

sermon.title: Discipleship in 3D, Part One
sermon.why: Part of Begg's series A Study in 2 Timothy, this message works through 2 Timothy 2:3-6, the images of the soldier, athlete, and farmer, drawing out the single-minded focus, disciplined obedience, and patient toil that mark faithful endurance in Christ's service.

quiz.q: Where does Timothy find the strength Paul calls him to?

options.text: In the grace that is in Christ Jesus, received rather than self-generated.
options.note: The verb is passive: be strengthened in grace, not by willpower.

options.text: In his own determination and natural courage.
options.note: Paul locates the strength in grace, not in Timothy's resolve.

options.text: In the support of the many faithful teachers around him.
options.note: Faithful teachers matter, but the strength named here is grace in Christ.

options.text: In God's empowering, which he is to draw on for endurance.
options.note: True and close, though the verse specifically names the grace in Christ Jesus.

quiz.q: What is the point of the soldier, athlete, and farmer images?

options.text: Faithful gospel work calls for focus, discipline, and hard, patient labor.
options.note: Together the three picture single-minded, disciplined, diligent endurance.

options.text: Ministry should be easy and free of hardship.
options.note: Each image assumes hardship, rules, and toil, not ease.

options.text: Christians should literally take up soldiering, athletics, or farming.
options.note: These are illustrations of endurance, not literal vocations to adopt.

options.text: Serving Christ requires endurance and self-denial to please Him.
options.note: True in substance, though it slightly narrows the threefold picture of focus, discipline, and toil.

quiz.q: How does the gospel's spread relate to Paul's chains?

options.text: Paul is chained, but the word of God cannot be chained.
options.note: Verse 9 contrasts Paul's bondage with the unstoppable word.

options.text: Paul's imprisonment has silenced the gospel for now.
options.note: The opposite: the word runs free even as Paul is bound.

options.text: The gospel spreads only when preachers are free from suffering.
options.note: Paul endures suffering precisely so the elect may be saved.

options.text: Paul endures all things so the elect may obtain salvation and glory.
options.note: True and stated in verse 10, though the sharp point is that the word itself cannot be chained.

quiz.q: What does Paul most want Timothy to remember at the center of it all?

options.text: Jesus Christ, raised from the dead and descended from David.
options.note: Verse 8 puts the risen Christ, the offspring of David, at the heart.

options.text: The rules that athletes must follow to win.
options.note: That is one illustration, not the center; the center is the risen Christ.

options.text: His own achievements in ministry.
options.note: Paul points away from himself to the risen Jesus.

options.text: The gospel Paul preaches, summed up in the living Lord.
options.note: True, and that gospel is exactly Christ raised from the dead.

quiz.q: What does verse 13 teach about God when we are faithless?

options.text: He remains faithful, because He cannot deny Himself.
options.note: God's faithfulness rests on His own unchanging character.

options.text: He becomes faithless toward us in return.
options.note: The verse says the opposite: He remains faithful.

options.text: His faithfulness depends on how faithful we manage to be.
options.note: Paul roots His faithfulness in Himself, not in our performance.

options.text: His steadfastness holds firm even when ours fails.
options.note: True and comforting, though the ground given is that He cannot deny Himself.

questions: Paul tells Timothy to be strong in grace, not in himself. Where are you trying to endure on willpower instead of drawing on the grace that is in Christ?
The gospel travels from Paul to Timothy to faithful people to others still. Who taught you the faith, and to whom are you entrusting it now?
The soldier keeps free of entangling distractions to please his commander. What lesser concerns are dividing your focus from Christ right now?
Remembering the risen Christ steadied Paul in chains. How would fixing your mind on the living Jesus change the hardship you are facing this week?
When we are faithless, He remains faithful. How does resting your security in God's faithfulness rather than your own change the way you follow Him?

translationNotes.note: Be strong translates a passive verb, be strengthened, pointing to strength received in the grace of Christ rather than summoned from within.
Raised from the dead is in the perfect tense, stressing an accomplished event with abiding result: Christ was raised and remains the living Lord.
The trustworthy saying of verses 11 to 13 is widely thought to be an early Christian hymn or confession; its balanced lines are rendered here as clean prose.
Not part of this movement, but note that some manuscripts read the Lord in place of God, as the BSB footnote observes.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 2 Timothy 2:1-13. The poetic line breaks in verses 11 to 13 have been rendered as prose.
